newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-SAMARANCH ATTACKS NAGANO OVER DOWNHILL START.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SAMARANCH ATTACKS NAGANO OVER DOWNHILL START.

text.p: International Olympic Committee (IOC) chief Juan Antonio Samaranch on Tuesday attacked the organisers of next year's Nagano Winter Olympics for refusing to solve a bitter row over the showpiece event, the Alpine skiing downhill.
Japanese organisers are presently battling with the International Ski Federation (FIS) who want the downhill starting point put further up the slope because the run will be too short.
But Nagano chiefs have refused, saying it would break environmental laws because it would take the start into a national park.
But Samaranch said: "Thousands of skiers use this zone during the weekend. The zone is not protected...It is not easy to understand, even for myself...The FIS is still insisting for change."
Although Samaranch stressed in an interview that he was very happy with the preparations for the Games next February, it is clear that the dispute has tarnished Nagano's image internationally.
Even Japanese Olympic officials have been pushing organisers to raise the start from 1,680 metres.

Samaranch was speaking at the world athletics championships less than a month before he stands for re-election as IOC president in Lausanne where the venue for the 2004 Summer Games will also be decided.

The IOC's process of choosing the city has been criticised as too tedious. In the 2004 bidding race, about 11 cities were allowed to apply before a final short list of five was drawn up to go to a vote of the IOC congress next month.
But Samaranch said: "We are not going to change the system during my period in office...We can't put a limit on it. Not accepting a bid is impossible."
Athens, the host of the world championships, is bidding with Rome, Cape Town, Stockholm and Buenos Aires to stage the 2004 Games.
The five cities were put on the final list earlier this year after IOC officials visited the 11 cities and wrote a detailed report on the technical aspects of their bids.
